title: Prosecutor v. Prlić et al. — destruction of the Old Bridge of Mostar
question: Did the destruction of the Old Bridge of Mostar in November 1993 constitute wanton destruction of cities, towns or villages, or devastation not justified by military necessity, as a violation of the laws or customs of war?
facts: In 1993 the HVO (Croatian Defence Council) and the ABiH (Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina) were fighting in and around Mostar, where the HVO had laid siege to East Mostar. Throughout the day on 8 November 1993, an HVO tank fired at the Old Bridge of Mostar, a sixteenth-century bridge over the Neretva river; by the evening the bridge was on the verge of collapse, and it was destroyed. The Trial Chamber found that the bridge was used by the ABiH for combat activities and that its destruction would cut off practically all possibilities for the ABiH to continue its supply operations in the area. The destruction resulted in the virtually total isolation of certain residents of the area and had a significant psychological impact on the Muslim population of Mostar. The Trial Chamber also found that the HVO destroyed the bridge in order to sap the morale of the Muslim population.
holding: In its Appeals Judgement of 29 November 2017, the ICTY Appeals Chamber, Judge Pocar dissenting, held that since the Old Bridge was a military target at the time of the attack, and its destruction thus offered a definite military advantage, it could not be considered, in and of itself, as wanton destruction not justified by military necessity. In the absence of any destruction of property not justified by military necessity in the Trial Chamber's legal findings, a requisite element of the crime was not satisfied, and the Appeals Chamber overturned the finding that destroying the Old Bridge constituted wanton destruction of cities, towns or villages, or devastation not justified by military necessity. It also reversed the findings that the destruction constituted persecution and the unlawful infliction of terror on civilians.
key_reasoning: The Trial Chamber had itself found that the bridge was a military target at the time of the attack, because its destruction would cut off practically all possibilities for the ABiH to continue its supply operations.

Because the bridge was a military target, its destruction offered a definite military advantage and could not in and of itself be wanton destruction not justified by military necessity; the Trial Chamber's proportionality reasoning did not supply the missing element.
Without any destruction of property not justified by military necessity in the legal findings, a requisite element of the crime was not satisfied.

Given the findings that the HVO had a military interest in destroying the bridge and that it was a military target, no reasonable trier of fact could find the specific intent to discriminate or to spread terror, so the persecution and terror findings for the bridge were also reversed (Judge Pocar dissenting).
